essence: Leandra is guarded by two species of tiny household gods, the Penates who live by the front door and move with the family and the Lares who live in the kitchen and stay with the house, and each species is sure that it alone is the real Leandra.
textDetails: Leandra is protected by gods of two species, both invisibly small and uncountably many.
Species one lives just inside each house's front door, beside the coat rack and the umbrella stand.
When the household moves, these door gods go along and take up residence in the new home as soon as the keys change hands.
Species two keeps to the kitchen, favouring the space under the pots, the chimney hood or flue, and the broom cupboard.
Kitchen gods are part of the building: when a family moves out, they stay on with whoever moves in.
They may predate the house itself, having lurked among the weeds of the empty building plot inside a rusty tin can.
Should the house be demolished and replaced by a vast apartment block for fifty families, they reappear, multiplied, in all fifty kitchens.
Marco calls the door gods Penates and the kitchen gods Lares.

Within one house the species mingle, pay calls, promenade together along stucco cornices and radiator pipes, gossip about the family, squabble readily or keep the peace for years; in a line-up they are indistinguishable.

Lares have watched Penates of every background and habit come and go; newcomer Penates must squeeze in beside proud Lares from grand but decaying palaces or prickly, mistrustful Lares from tin shanties.
What Leandra really is remains endlessly disputed: the Penates think they are its soul, even the newest arrivals, and that Leandra goes with them when they emigrate.
The Lares regard the Penates as passing, pushy, meddling lodgers; for them the true Leandra is their own, the one that shapes everything inside it, older than the newcomers and bound to outlast them.

Both species grumble about everything that happens: the Penates hold up the elders, great-grandparents, great-aunts and the family as it used to be; the Lares hold up the neighbourhood before it was spoiled.
Both also scheme about the future: the Penates about the children's careers, the Lares about what the house or district could become if properly cared for.
Listen closely, above all at night, and the houses are full of them: rapid murmuring, interruptions, jibes, snorts and suppressed ironic giggles.
visualConcept: A night neighbourhood on a floating cobbled island, built as a ring of dollhouse cutaways: each house has its outer wall removed, so as the camera circles you look straight into lamp-lit entrance halls, kitchens and stairwells. The gods are shown exactly as the text has them, too small to see and too many to count: thousands of pinprick motes that only become visible as glowing dust under bloom. Penates are cool silver-cyan dust gathered just inside each front door around the coat rack and the umbrella stand; Lares are ember-orange dust packed under the pots on the stove, up inside the chimney hood and in the broom closet. Mixed single files of both species stroll along the stucco cornices and the radiator pipes, and while in line they fade to the same pale white, so in a row you cannot tell them apart. The neighbourhood is socially mixed: two decayed palaces with heavy cornices (their Lares slow, deep-glowing and haughty), ordinary three-storey houses, a fringe of corrugated tin shacks (their Lares jittery and flickering), a weedy vacant lot where a rusty can glows from within with Lares waiting for a house, and a fifty-family apartment block cut open like a honeycomb, every one of its fifty kitchens holding the same ember glow, multiplied. Families of tiny figures move house along the streets with handcarts, trailing rivers of silver dust, while the embers never leave their kitchens. The whole quarrel over whose city this is becomes visible at a glance as moving light against rooted light.
layout: Roughly circular floating island of dark cobbles, radius 20, with a ring street at r=11 and two cross streets meeting in a small central piazza. On the outer side of the ring stand the cutaway houses, open faces pointing outward toward the orbiting camera and front doors opening onto the ring street: 10 ordinary houses (2-3 floors, 3 wide by 2.5 deep, floor height 0.6, doors 0.45 tall), 2 decayed palaces (4 floors, 5.5 wide, peeling ochre stucco, deep cornices on every floor), and 6 tin shacks clustered on the south-east edge (one room, 1.2 by 1.2, 0.8 tall, corrugated tin, a stovepipe). Every interior reuses one instanced prop kit: an entrance hall with coat rack and umbrella stand beside the door; a kitchen with stove, three pots, a chimney hood rising into a flue and a broom closet with its door ajar; radiator pipes along the walls; stucco cornice moulding under each ceiling. Inside the ring: the fifty-family block (10 bays by 5 floors, 11 long, 3.5 deep, 3.5 tall) cut open on the side facing the default camera as a honeycomb of 50 identical apartments, with 50 lit kitchen windows on its far side; the vacant lot (4 by 4, tall instanced weeds, a rusty can 0.15 tall); 4 street lamps in the piazza. Particle budget about 10,000 points (additive THREE.Points): 60-150 Penates per front door, 80-200 Lares per kitchen, 40 per kitchen in the block, 120 in the rusty can. 30-40 tiny people and 2 handcarts.
signatureMotion: 1) Household murmur: every cluster jitters in Brownian motion and pulses in irregular, speech-like rhythms; small arcs of sparks hop between neighbouring clusters (quips), the odd puff bursts outward (a huff), and now and then a whole room flickers in sync (stifled laughter). 2) Strolls: single files of mixed motes walk the cornice lines and radiator pipes, cross-fading from their species colour to a shared pale white while in line and back again as they peel off home. 3) A move, every 25 s or so: a family of 3-4 figures leaves a house with a handcart and walks the streets to an empty house; a comet tail of silver Penates follows them out of the door and, when a tiny gold key glints at the new threshold, pours in and settles round the new coat rack; the old house goes dark except for its ember kitchen, which flares warily when the next family arrives with Penates of a slightly different tint.
interactionDescription: Starts a city-wide moving day. Families pour out of every house at once with carts and bundles; each family's silver Penates stream behind it in rivers of light that criss-cross the ring street, while every ember Lar stays exactly where it was, in kitchens, chimney hoods and broom closets, in the palaces and the tin shacks, in the rusty can and the fifty kitchens of the block. A few families walk off the island's edge along a faint path into the void, carrying their Penates, who are sure they are taking Leandra with them, and newcomers arrive out of the dark with Penates in subtly different tints of silver. Toggle off and everyone settles: keys glint, the silver dust gathers by the new doors, and the two species start murmuring together again.
mood: Late evening after supper, mild and still, a faint blue mist lying at street level. Deep blue night outside; warm amber lamplight inside every cutaway room, so the island glows like a cabinet of lit dollhouses. Street lamps make small pools on cobbles that look slightly damp. Intimate, gossipy and a little comic, with a soft, constant murmur of light.
caption: Every house in Leandra is guarded twice, by gods no one has ever seen or managed to count. Those by the front door, among the coats and umbrellas, pack up and follow the family to each new address. Those in the kitchen, under the pans and up the chimney, belong to the walls and may have been there before them. Each kind claims to be the real Leandra; after dark the houses fill with their bickering.
motto: Some gods follow the family; others wait for the next one.
camera: Distance about 27, elevation about 22 degrees, target (0, 1.5, 0), framed so two cutaway houses fill the foreground with the block's honeycomb of fifty kitchens glowing behind them; slightly long lens (field of view about 35 degrees) for a dollhouse look under the tilt-shift; slow orbit, one turn per 4 minutes, so every cutaway passes in turn.
